rv.q: Martin Shaw’s finely tuned More is credible both as fallible human and as hero – loving to family and friends, exasperated by fools and villains, lawyerly in his discretion, firm in his adherence to conscience (well-known to television audiences as Judge John Deed, Shaw previously played More on stage in 2006).
Jonathan Church’s new touring production is smart and handsome but feels like an old-fashioned history play, creaky in parts though still an ultimately moving portrait of quiet heroism.
History’s slipperiness is captured in Jonathan Church’s new staging of Robert Bolt’s Tudor tale

This beautifully wrought production magnifies the ever repeating circle of power and destruction and will doubtless prompt many in the audience to muse on the fact that moral men rarely last long in politics.

This is a wonderful historical play but in the week that we saw Trump’s triumphant return to power in the US, the tale of political games playing, retaliatory actions and bold statements of patriotism and religious allegiance, the historical events in the play resonate strongly.
Director Jonathan Church faithfully delivers Bolt’s text in a production that is a joy for all lovers of historical drama.
A Man For All Seasons is a compelling historical play, rightfully rooted in realism, with Robert Bolt’s writing still just as strong sixty years later.
A Man for All Seasons is an unmissable, beautifully crafted theatrical experience that lingers in the mind long after the final bow.
